author: A Robot
objectives: Determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding domains and lone pairs.
Predict electron-domain geometry from steric number: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry when lone pairs are present.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and why they compress adjacent bond angles.
Apply VSEPR predictions to H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, and XeF4 and compare them with observed structures.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: Lewis Structures and Steric Number
modules.description: Students begin with a Lewis-structure view and learn to count electron domains around a central atom to determine steric number.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the central atom in a Lewis structure.
Count bonds and lone pairs as electron domains for VSEPR.
Calculate steric number as bonding domains plus lone pairs.
instructions: Place the AR scene on a clear tabletop.
Advance through the clips and watch electron domains appear around the central atom.
Remember that a single, double, or triple bond counts as one VSEPR domain.

components.text: Steric number = bonding domains + lone pairs

clips.changeMeaning: The central atom and Lewis-structure board appear to establish that VSEPR begins with a two-dimensional Lewis structure before predicting a three-dimensional shape.
clips.narration: VSEPR theory starts with a Lewis structure. Around the central atom, we count regions of electron density: bonds and lone pairs. These regions are called electron domains.

components.text: Bonding domains: 2\nMultiple bond = one VSEPR domain

clips.changeMeaning: Two blue bonding domains appear around the central atom to show how bonds in a Lewis structure become spatial electron domains in VSEPR.
clips.narration: First count bonding domains. Each direction from the central atom to another atom counts once, whether the bond is single, double, or triple.

clips.changeMeaning: A purple lone pair appears and the steric-number label updates to reinforce the calculation of steric number from all electron domains.
clips.narration: Now add the lone pairs on the central atom. With two bonding domains and one lone pair, the steric number is three.

modules.description: Electron domains rearrange in 3D to minimize repulsion, producing the five fundamental electron-domain geometries for steric numbers 2 through 6.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Match steric number 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 to the corresponding electron-domain geometry.
Identify ideal angles in the five parent geometries.
Describe VSEPR as a minimum-repulsion model.
instructions: Watch the same central atom gain different numbers of domains.
Observe how each domain set spreads out to reduce repulsions.
Use the label to connect steric number, geometry, and ideal bond angle.

clips.changeMeaning: Two opposite domains are enabled to model the linear geometry, connecting steric number two to a 180 degree arrangement.
clips.narration: With two electron domains, maximum separation is a straight line. Steric number two produces a linear electron-domain geometry with an ideal angle of 180 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: A third domain appears and all three domains move into a planar triangular arrangement, demonstrating trigonal planar electron-domain geometry.
clips.narration: With three electron domains, the lowest-repulsion arrangement is trigonal planar. The three domains lie in one plane, about 120 degrees apart.

clips.changeMeaning: Four domains reposition into a tetrahedral pattern, showing why steric number four requires a 3D structure rather than a flat square.
clips.narration: Four electron domains spread into a tetrahedron. This three-dimensional arrangement gives ideal angles of about 109.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: Five domains form three equatorial and two axial positions, highlighting that trigonal bipyramidal geometry contains different kinds of positions.
clips.narration: Five electron domains form a trigonal bipyramid. Three equatorial domains lie 120 degrees apart, while two axial domains sit above and below the plane.

clips.changeMeaning: A sixth domain appears to complete the octahedral set, with domains distributed along three perpendicular axes to minimize repulsion.
clips.narration: Six domains arrange octahedrally, with four positions in a square plane and one above and one below. Adjacent positions are 90 degrees apart.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3: Lone Pairs Change Molecular Geometry
modules.description: Shows how the electron-domain geometry includes all domains, while the molecular geometry names only the positions of atoms.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry.
Identify bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square pyramidal, and square planar shapes.
Explain why lone pairs are included in VSEPR counting but omitted from molecular-shape names.
instructions: Blue cylinders represent bonds to atoms; purple lobes represent lone pairs.
Compare the label for the parent electron-domain geometry with the visible molecular shape.
Notice that lone pairs occupy positions even though they are not atoms.

components.text: SN = 3: trigonal planar domains\nMolecular shape: bent

clips.changeMeaning: Two bonds and one lone pair form a trigonal planar domain set, while the label emphasizes that only the atoms define the bent molecular shape.
clips.narration: A steric number three atom with two bonds and one lone pair has trigonal planar electron-domain geometry, but the atoms form a bent molecular geometry.

components.text: SN = 4: tetrahedral domains\nMolecular shape: trigonal pyramidal

clips.changeMeaning: The domains move into a tetrahedral parent arrangement with three visible bonds and one lone pair, producing trigonal pyramidal geometry.
clips.narration: For steric number four, three bonds and one lone pair produce a trigonal pyramidal molecule. Ammonia is the classic example.

components.text: SN = 5: trigonal bipyramidal domains\n1 LP: seesaw | 2 LP: T-shaped

clips.changeMeaning: The central set becomes trigonal bipyramidal with an equatorial lone pair, visually showing the seesaw shape and labeling the related T-shaped case.
clips.narration: In trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry, lone pairs prefer equatorial positions. One lone pair gives a seesaw shape, and two equatorial lone pairs give a T-shaped molecule.

components.text: SN = 6: octahedral domains\n1 LP: square pyramidal | 2 LP: square planar

clips.changeMeaning: Four planar bonds and two opposite lone pairs appear from the octahedral parent geometry, demonstrating the square planar case and identifying the square pyramidal derivative.
clips.narration: For octahedral electron geometry, one lone pair gives square pyramidal geometry. Two opposite lone pairs leave four atoms in a square plane, producing square planar geometry.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Lone-Pair Repulsion and Bond Angles
modules.description: Compares methane and water to show why lone pairs compress bond angles below ideal tetrahedral values.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Rank electron-domain repulsions as lone pair-lone pair greater than lone pair-bonding pair greater than bonding pair-bonding pair.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs.
Compare methane's approximately 109.5 degree angle with water's approximately 104.5 degree H-O-H angle.
instructions: Compare the methane model on the left with the water model on the right.
Watch the purple lone-pair lobes and orange compression arrows appear.
Use the readout to connect repulsion strength to bond-angle deviation.

components.text: CH₄: tetrahedral, ~109.5°\nH₂O: tetrahedral domains, bent molecule

clips.changeMeaning: Methane and water are shown side by side so students can compare two steric-number-four molecules with different lone-pair counts.
clips.narration: Methane and water both have steric number four at the central atom. Methane has four bonding domains and is nearly ideal tetrahedral, with angles close to 109.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: Two enlarged lone-pair lobes appear on the water model, emphasizing that lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs.
clips.narration: Water has two bonding domains and two lone pairs. Lone pairs are closer to the central atom and occupy more angular space, so they repel bonding domains more strongly.

components.text: H–O–H ≈ 104.5°\nLone pairs compress bond angle below 109.5°

clips.changeMeaning: Inward arrows appear and the readout changes to show that lone-pair repulsion compresses water's H-O-H angle below 109.5 degrees.
clips.narration: The lone pairs push the O-H bonding domains closer together. The water bond angle is compressed to about 104.5 degrees, smaller than the ideal tetrahedral angle.

modules.moduleName: Scene 5: VSEPR Predictions for Real Molecules
modules.description: A molecule gallery applies the complete VSEPR workflow to water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, and XeF4.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict molecular geometries for H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, and XeF4.
Connect steric number, electron-domain geometry, lone-pair count, and molecular geometry.
Compare VSEPR predictions to commonly observed molecular structures.
instructions: Scan the gallery from left to right as molecules appear.
Read the summary label for steric number and molecular shape.
Use the final clip to review the VSEPR prediction workflow.

components.text: SN = 4 examples\nH₂O: bent | NH₃: trigonal pyramidal | CH₄: tetrahedral

clips.changeMeaning: Water, ammonia, and methane appear together to show how lone-pair count changes molecular geometry within the same tetrahedral electron-domain family.
clips.narration: For steric number four, the electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral. Water has two lone pairs and is bent. Ammonia has one lone pair and is trigonal pyramidal. Methane has no lone pairs and is tetrahedral.

components.text: PF₅: SN = 5, trigonal bipyramidal\nSF₆: SN = 6, octahedral

clips.changeMeaning: PF5 and SF6 appear as examples where no lone pairs are present on the central atom, so molecular geometry matches the electron-domain geometry.
clips.narration: Phosphorus pentafluoride has five bonding domains and no lone pairs, so it is trigonal bipyramidal. Sulfur hexafluoride has six bonding domains and no lone pairs, so it is octahedral.

components.text: Workflow: count domains → electron geometry → lone pairs → molecular shape\nXeF₄: SN = 6, square planar

clips.changeMeaning: XeF4 appears and the label summarizes the complete VSEPR workflow from domain counting through the observed molecular shape.
clips.narration: Xenon tetrafluoride has six electron domains: four Xe-F bonds and two lone pairs. The lone pairs occupy opposite positions, leaving four fluorine atoms in a square plane. Its observed square planar structure matches the VSEPR prediction.
